items.title: AFLW grand final: gap closes on three-peat chasing Kangaroos as Demons seek upset
items.summary:
North Melbourne are out to secure their legacy but in their way stands a confident Melbourne side ready for their biggest test of the season

The early chapters of the record books are still being written as the AFLW enters its second decade with North Melbourne now just one win away from a milestone that could stand the test of time. The Kangaroos have become the league’s benchmark during a dominant three seasons, and last year raised the bar higher as the first club to claim back-to-back premierships. A third consecutive grand final triumph when they face Melbourne at a sold out Ikon Park on Friday night would earn the Roos a larger slice of history – and cement their place as the competition’s first dynasty.

The North Melbourne juggernaut has raised the standard of the AFLW; the Roos have lost only once since being defeated by Brisbane in the 2023 grand final, then turned the tables on the same rivals to win in the past two deciders. They romped through another campaign to finish the league’s 11th season as minor premiers with 11 victories and a percentage of 246.6%, though their record-breaking winning streak ended at 32 matches with a surprise loss to Hawthorn.

items.summary:
Crystal Palace’s influential supporters’ group disbanded 24 hours before their first home game this season – and Selhurst Park has not been the same since

Simon Teesdale could not help feeling mixed emotions when his beloved Crystal Palace won the Conference League in Leipzig in May. He started going to Selhurst Park with his father in the 1980s, became a season-ticket holder in the 1990s and has watched with pride as the club established itself as a permanent fixture in the Premier League over the past 14 years. Palace finally secured a major trophy in the 2025 FA Cup final – an experience Teesdale remembers as “one of the best days of my life” – and followed that up by winning the Conference League but he decided in August not to renew his season ticket.

“Something happened between the FA Cup win and today that changed me,” he wrote in an emotional article published last month on his website. “Tipped me over the edge. Actually, it’s fairer to say that something accelerated in that period of time. The seeds were sown years ago.”

items.title: Alejandro Garnacho and the curious case of Aston Villa’s outcast loanees | Ben Fisher
items.summary:
Unai Emery wanted the winger but, like Harvey Elliott last season, he has been left out in the cold despite Villa’s attacking struggles

It is three years this week since Alejandro Garnacho opened the scoring for Manchester United in a 3-3 draw at Galatasaray in the Champions League, on a typically boisterous night in Istanbul when Victor Lindelöf and Aaron Wan-Bissaka, now his teammates at Aston Villa, were also among the starters. At the time, Garnacho was a teenage star flourishing on the grandest of stages, a fixture in the United team and fresh from scoring an outrageous overhead kick at Goodison Park a few days earlier that would later clinch the Premier League’s goal-of-the-season award.

He went on to score twice at Old Trafford on Boxing Day, in a 3-2 victory against Villa, and a couple of months later his double at home to West Ham was the catalyst for that iconic celebration photo of Garnacho, Kobbie Mainoo and Rasmus Højlund sitting on the advertising hoardings at the Stretford End, beaming smiles all round. All three were at the heart of United’s plans for a bright future, beacons of hope. At the end of that season, Garnacho signed off in style, he and Mainoo scoring against Manchester City at Wembley to win the FA Cup.
items.t: Alejandro Garnacho and the curious case of Aston Villa’s outcast loanees | Ben Fisher

  • England in home dressing room against All Blacks

The Rugby Football Union’s head groundsman is confident Twickenham’s pitch will hold up to staging six matches across three days for the Nations Championship finals, detailing the lengths to which he and his support staff will go.

In preparation for the showpiece weekend, the turf – which had been in place since 2012 – was ripped up over the summer with a new state-of-the-art hybrid surface laid. It comes complete with a reservoir that can hold 1.4m litres of water below it – which can be reused using nanobubble technology – and was grown in Scunthorpe before being transported to south-west London.

items.title: ‘It’s stressful but better than having a proper job’: the life of a cricket umpire
items.summary:
Four umpires discuss how they deal with players, why they avoid social media, how technology is changing cricket and why umpiring beats being a football referee

By Wisden Cricket Monthly

Last summer, sat in a quiet ground at the fag-end of a four-dayer, with a few souls still kicking around and a clutch of cameras streaming what was left of the day live on YouTube, it struck me again what a great, strange sanctuary this place is, out there on the edges of the modern world. The game is trying to move, albeit at its own pace. Later that night, the day’s highlights would be landing on social media, available to all, for the game’s devotees to pore over and pick apart.

More people are watching the County Championship than ever before. Streaming numbers show a growing audience in the UK and a widening uptake across the cricketing globe. The numbers aren’t yet earth-shattering, but how could they be, with such eccentric fare?
